blocks.text: A galvanised steel bucket and a copper pipe sit in the same damp plant room. Within a year a bright steel bolt that joins the pipe clamp to the steel bracket has a hole eaten through its thread, while the copper is untouched. Corrosion looks chaotic, but it is governed by a simple electrical circuit: two half-reactions, a pathway for ions and a path for electrons.

blocks.markdown: Corrosion of a metal in water is an **electrochemical** process. The metal gives up electrons at one site, and those electrons are consumed at another site by a different reaction. Both reactions must run at the same total rate, because electrons cannot accumulate. This single balance explains why corrosion needs an electrolyte, why it depends on oxygen, and why joining two different metals can accelerate it.

blocks.title: Anode, cathode and electrolyte
blocks.text: The **anode** is where metal is oxidised (loses electrons) and dissolves. The **cathode** is where a species in the solution is reduced (gains electrons); the cathode metal itself does not corrode. The **electrolyte** carries ions between them, and a metallic path carries electrons. Remove any of the four parts (anode, cathode, electrolyte, electron path) and corrosion stops.

blocks.caption: Iron dissolves at the anode, and either oxygen reduction (aerated water) or hydrogen evolution (acid) takes the electrons at the cathode. Fe2+ and OH- then form Fe(OH)2, which oxidises to rust.

blocks.markdown: On a single piece of steel, anodic and cathodic sites may both exist on the same surface, separated by micrometres (a differently stressed grain, a scratch, a patch of scale). Rust then forms where the ions meet, which is often away from the site where the metal was dissolved. If oxygen cannot reach the surface (deaerated water) the cathodic reaction is starved and the corrosion rate falls to a very low level.

rows: Corrode in preference to everything below
Used for sacrificial anodes and galvanising
Corrode when coupled to steel or copper
Corrode when coupled to copper alloys or stainless steel
Protected when coupled to steel or zinc; cathodes
Cathodes; the more active partner suffers
Strongly accelerate corrosion of any metal they touch
blocks.caption: A simplified galvanic series, from most active (top) to most noble (bottom). The real series depends on the electrolyte and surface condition.

blocks.markdown: **The galvanic series.** When two different metals are in electrical contact in a common electrolyte, the one higher in the series (more active) becomes the anode and corrodes faster, while the one lower in the series (more noble) becomes the cathode and is protected. Any couple can be predicted from the table: zinc and steel corrode zinc; steel and copper corrode steel. The series gives the *direction* of attack but not its *rate*; the rate depends on the area ratio, the electrolyte conductivity and the polarisation of each metal.

blocks.title: Unfavourable area ratio
blocks.text: The galvanic current is shared over the anode area. A **small anode coupled to a large cathode** carries a large current density and corrodes very quickly (a steel bolt in a copper plate). A **large anode with a small cathode** spreads the same current over a large area, so each square centimetre corrodes slowly (a copper rivet in a steel plate).

blocks.caption: Faraday's law. i is the corrosion current density (A per cm^2), M the molar mass (g per mol), n the number of electrons per atom, F = 96485 C per mol, rho the density (g per cm^3). Penetration rate r is in cm per second, convertible to mm per year with 1 year is about 31.56 million seconds.

blocks.title: Corrosion rate of steel from the corrosion current
blocks.prompt: Iron ($M=55.85$ g mol$^{-1}$, $n=2$, $\rho=7.87$ g cm$^{-3}$) corrodes uniformly in a solution with a corrosion current density of $25\ \mu$A cm$^{-2}$. Find the penetration rate in mm per year.

steps.text: Convert the current density to A per cm$^2$ and compute the mass loss per unit area per second.
Divide by the density to obtain the penetration rate in cm per second.
Convert to mm per year using $3.156\times10^{7}$ s per year and 10 mm per cm.

blocks.answer: About 0.29 mm per year (so 1 microamp per square centimetre is about 0.0116 mm per year for iron).

blocks.title: Galvanic couple and area ratio
blocks.prompt: A steel bolt of exposed area 3 cm$^2$ clamps a large copper plate in a wet environment, and carries a total galvanic current of 0.60 mA, all of which is anodic dissolution of the steel. Use the iron constants above. Find the penetration rate of the bolt, and compare with a copper rivet in a steel plate of exposed steel area 600 cm$^2$ carrying the same current.

steps.text: Steel is more active than copper, so the steel is the anode and copper the cathode. For the bolt, the current density is the current divided by the anode area.
Use the iron factor 0.0116 mm per year per $\mu$A cm$^{-2}$.
For the copper rivet in the steel plate the same current is spread over 600 cm$^2$ of steel: $i=1.0\ \mu$A cm$^{-2}$, so the penetration rate is $1.0\times0.0116=0.012$ mm per year, 200 times slower.

blocks.answer: The small steel bolt loses about 2.3 mm per year, whereas the large steel plate loses about 0.012 mm per year; the area ratio makes a 200-fold difference.

blocks.title: Two questions for any couple
blocks.text: First ask which metal is more active in the series to find the anode. Then ask what the area ratio and the electrolyte are, because those decide how fast it corrodes. Protection can be achieved by insulating the metals electrically, choosing metals close together in the series, or making the anode area large.

points: Corrosion is a pair of half-reactions: oxidation of the metal at the anode and reduction of oxygen or hydrogen ions at the cathode, at equal rates, so removing oxygen, electrolyte or the electron path stops it.
In a bimetallic couple the more active metal in the galvanic series becomes the anode and corrodes; a small anode with a large cathode corrodes fastest.
Faraday's law $r=iM/(nF\rho)$ converts a corrosion current density to a penetration rate; for iron, 1 $\mu$A cm$^{-2}$ corresponds to about 0.0116 mm per year.

questions.stem: Iron is corroding in aerated, neutral water. Which pair of half-reactions describes the process?

options.text: Anode: O$_2$ + 2H$_2$O + 4e$^{-}$ $\rightarrow$ 4OH$^{-}$; cathode: Fe $\rightarrow$ Fe$^{2+}$ + 2e$^{-}$
Anode: Fe$^{2+}$ + 2e$^{-}$ $\rightarrow$ Fe; cathode: 2H$^{+}$ + 2e$^{-}$ $\rightarrow$ H$_2$
Anode: Fe $\rightarrow$ Fe$^{2+}$ + 2e$^{-}$; cathode: O$_2$ + 2H$_2$O + 4e$^{-}$ $\rightarrow$ 4OH$^{-}$
Anode: 2H$_2$O $\rightarrow$ O$_2$ + 4H$^{+}$ + 4e$^{-}$; cathode: Fe $\rightarrow$ Fe$^{2+}$ + 2e$^{-}$

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: this swaps the roles; oxidation of the metal always occurs at the anode.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the first reaction is a reduction of iron ions (deposition) and the cathodic reaction is that of acid, not neutral water.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: iron is oxidised at the anode, and dissolved oxygen is reduced at the cathode in aerated neutral water.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: both reactions are mis-assigned; oxygen is consumed, not produced, in corrosion.

questions.explanation: Corrosion needs oxidation (metal loses electrons) at the anode, and reduction of an oxidant at the cathode. In aerated neutral water the oxidant is dissolved oxygen, which is reduced to hydroxide ions.

questions.stem: A steel pipe full of neutral water corrodes extremely slowly after the oxygen is removed from the water by a chemical scavenger. Why?

options.text: The cathodic reaction has nothing to reduce, so the electrons released at the anode cannot be consumed and the overall rate falls
The steel becomes the cathode of a cell and is protected by the scavenger
The anodic reaction is blocked because Fe$^{2+}$ cannot form in deaerated water
The electrolyte becomes an electrical insulator

questions.correctOptionText: The cathodic reaction has nothing to reduce, so the electrons released at the anode cannot be consumed and the overall rate falls

distractorRationale.a: Correct: anodic and cathodic rates must be equal, and the cathodic reduction of oxygen limits the whole process.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a scavenger removes the oxidant; it does not turn the steel into a cathode.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: iron can still dissolve, but the electrons would have no acceptor.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: removing oxygen does not change the ionic conductivity of the water.

questions.explanation: The anodic and cathodic reactions are coupled by electron conservation, so the slower one limits the corrosion rate. With the oxygen gone, the cathodic reduction of oxygen cannot take place, so anodic dissolution is also suppressed.

questions.stem: A zinc plate is bolted to a copper plate in seawater. Using the galvanic series, which statement is correct?

options.text: Copper is the more active metal, so it becomes the anode and corrodes
Both metals corrode at equal rates, since both are in contact with the same seawater
Neither metal corrodes, because they are in direct electrical contact
Zinc is the more active metal, so it becomes the anode and corrodes while the copper is protected

questions.correctOptionText: Zinc is the more active metal, so it becomes the anode and corrodes while the copper is protected

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: copper is more noble than zinc and acts as the cathode.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: a couple makes one metal corrode faster and the other slower, not equally.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: contact provides the electron path that lets the galvanic cell operate.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: zinc is higher in the series (more active) and corrodes preferentially.

questions.explanation: In the galvanic series zinc lies above copper, so it has the more negative potential and becomes the anode. Zinc dissolves and the copper acts as the cathode, which is the principle used by sacrificial zinc anodes.

questions.stem: Four galvanic couples of steel and copper are exposed to the same wet environment. Which is likely to cause the fastest penetration of the steel?

options.text: A large steel sheet with a small copper rivet
A small steel fastener in a large copper sheet
Equal areas of steel and copper
A steel sheet with a copper coating that is intact

questions.correctOptionText: A small steel fastener in a large copper sheet

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the current is spread over a large steel area, so penetration is slow.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the same galvanic current is concentrated on a small anode area, giving a very high current density.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: equal areas give a moderate current density.
distractorRationale.d: Wrong: an intact coating separates the steel from the electrolyte so no galvanic cell forms.

questions.explanation: Penetration rate is proportional to anodic current density, which is the galvanic current divided by the anode area. A small anode coupled to a large cathode therefore corrodes the fastest.

questions.stem: What does the galvanic series tell the engineer about a couple of two metals?

options.text: The corrosion rate of the anode in mm per year
The exact potential difference in every electrolyte
Which metal has the higher density
Which metal is the anode and corrodes preferentially, but not how fast it corrodes

questions.correctOptionText: Which metal is the anode and corrodes preferentially, but not how fast it corrodes

distractorRationale.a: Wrong: the rate also depends on area ratio, conductivity and polarisation, which the series does not include.
distractorRationale.b: Wrong: the series is specific to a given electrolyte, such as seawater.
distractorRationale.c: Wrong: density is unrelated to the galvanic series.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the series gives the direction of galvanic attack only.

questions.explanation: The galvanic series ranks metals by corrosion potential in a given electrolyte, so it tells us which one is the anode. The rate must be estimated from the current density through Faraday's law.

questions.stem: Zinc ($M=65.38$ g mol$^{-1}$, $n=2$, $\rho=7.14$ g cm$^{-3}$) on a roof corrodes uniformly with a corrosion current density of $4\ \mu$A cm$^{-2}$. Using $F=96485$ C mol$^{-1}$ and 1 year $=3.156\times10^{7}$ s, find the penetration rate in mm per year.
questions.explanation: The mass loss rate is $4\times10^{-6}\times65.38/(2\times96485)=1.355\times10^{-9}$ g cm$^{-2}$ s$^{-1}$. Dividing by $\rho$ gives $1.898\times10^{-10}$ cm s$^{-1}$, which is $1.898\times10^{-10}\times3.156\times10^{7}\times10=0.060$ mm per year.

questions.stem: A steel water tank has a wetted area of 150 cm$^2$ corroding at a uniform corrosion current density of $15\ \mu$A cm$^{-2}$. Using $M=55.85$ g mol$^{-1}$, $n=2$, $F=96485$ C mol$^{-1}$ and 1 year $=3.156\times10^{7}$ s, find the mass of iron lost in one year, in grams.
questions.explanation: The total current is $15\times10^{-6}\times150=2.25\times10^{-3}$ A, so the charge passed in a year is $2.25\times10^{-3}\times3.156\times10^{7}=7.10\times10^{4}$ C. Faraday's law gives $m=QM/(nF)=7.10\times10^{4}\times55.85/(2\times96485)=20.5$ g.

questions.stem: A steel rivet of exposed area 2.5 cm$^2$ is in contact with a large copper sheet and carries a galvanic current of 0.45 mA, all through anodic dissolution of the iron. Using $M=55.85$ g mol$^{-1}$, $n=2$, $\rho=7.87$ g cm$^{-3}$, $F=96485$ C mol$^{-1}$ and 1 year $=3.156\times10^{7}$ s, find the penetration rate of the rivet in mm per year.
questions.explanation: The anodic current density is $0.45\times10^{-3}/2.5=1.8\times10^{-4}$ A cm$^{-2}$, which is $180\ \mu$A cm$^{-2}$. Faraday's law then gives $r=180\times10^{-6}\times55.85/(2\times96485\times7.87)=6.62\times10^{-9}$ cm s$^{-1}$, which is $2.09$ mm per year.

questions.stem: Explain corrosion of iron in aerated seawater as a pair of half-reactions. Write the anodic and cathodic reactions, state which reaction limits the rate, and describe why rust forms away from the point at which iron dissolves.
markingGuide: Electrons flow through the metal and ions through the electrolyte; the two reactions must run at equal rates
The cathodic reaction, supply of oxygen to the surface, normally limits the rate in aerated neutral water
Fe$^{2+}$ and OH$^{-}$ meet in the solution and form Fe(OH)$_2$, which oxidises to rust, so the rust forms between anodic and cathodic sites rather than at the anode
Removing any of the four elements (anode, cathode, electrolyte, electron path) stops corrosion
questions.explanation: Corrosion is an electrochemical cell short-circuited on one piece of metal. The anodic and cathodic sites are separated, so the products meet in the solution, and the slower reaction controls the rate.

questions.stem: An aluminium alloy plate is fastened with passive stainless steel bolts in a marine environment. Predict which metal corrodes using the galvanic series and discuss how the area ratio affects the rate. If the galvanic current is 1.0 mA, the exposed aluminium area is 5 cm$^2$, $M=26.98$ g mol$^{-1}$, $n=3$ and $\rho=2.70$ g cm$^{-3}$, estimate the penetration rate of the aluminium in mm per year.
markingGuide: Aluminium is more active (anodic) than passive stainless steel, so aluminium corrodes and the stainless steel is the cathode

Rate depends on current density at the anode, i.e. the current divided by the exposed anode area; small anode with large cathode is worst, so a large aluminium plate with small stainless bolts is more tolerable
Faraday's law $r=iM/(nF\rho)$ gives about $6.9\times10^{-9}$ cm s$^{-1}$
Converts to about 2.2 mm per year
Possible mitigation: insulate the bolts from the plate, use compatible metals, coat the cathode, or apply sealant
questions.explanation: The more active metal in the couple, aluminium, is the anode. With a current density of 200 $\mu$A cm$^{-2}$, Faraday's law gives $r=200\times10^{-6}\times26.98/(3\times96485\times2.70)=6.9\times10^{-9}$ cm s$^{-1}$, which is 2.2 mm per year.
